questions.problem:
$$
\,x=\,b
$$

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the matrix equation above gives the least-squares solution of $Ax=b.$ From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ R\,\,x & ={Q}^{T}\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are $R$ and ${Q}^{T}.$

questions.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}],\,R=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 6 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 6 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}33 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=33 \\ 2{x}_{2}=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-3.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-5(-3) & =33 \\ 3{x}_{1} & =18 \\ {x}_{1} & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 & \sqrt{2} \\ 2 & -\sqrt{2} \\ 1 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,R=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ \sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}20 \\ -4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=20 \\ 2\sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=-4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-(-2) & =20 \\ 2{x}_{1} & =18 \\ {x}_{1} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}-7 & 24 \\ -24 & -7\end{aligned}],\,R=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ is orthogonal, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}-7 & -24 \\ 24 & -7\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-11 \\ {x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-(2) & =-11 \\ {x}_{1} & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

$$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ is orthogonal, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 7 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & 7 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+7{x}_{2}=5 \\ 5{x}_{2}=5.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+7(1) & =5 \\ {x}_{1} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

$$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}3\sqrt{2} & -3\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{3} & \sqrt{3} & 0\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}3\sqrt{2} & -3\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}15\sqrt{2} \\ 6\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}3\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}-3\sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=15\sqrt{2} \\ 2\sqrt{3}{x}_{2}=6\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.problem:
$$
\bbox[5px, border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{A}} \, \mathbf{x} = \bbox[5px, border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{A}} \, \mathbf{b}
$$

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the matrix equation above gives the least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}.$ From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
A^T A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b}.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, it satisfies $Q^T Q = I,$ and we get

$$
R^T R \mathbf{x} = R^T \! Q^T \mathbf{b}.
$$

Finally, since $R^T$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $(R^T)^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ \,R\,\,x & ={Q}^{T}\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are $R$ and $Q^T.$
